content: Consumable costs and staffing expenses collectively accounted for 96% of the unit costs associated with both PrePex and surgical voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) procedures. In Mozambique, these two cost categories contributed to 86% and 63% of the unit costs for PrePex and surgical methods, respectively, as reported by Schutte in 2016. Consumables and staffing costs are the primary cost drivers for VMMC. Compared to the surgical method, device-based approaches, such as PrePex, involve shorter procedure durations, which reduce the cost of clinician time. However, the additional costs of the device itself, associated medical supplies, and subsequent device removal inflate the overall cost of the device-based approach. The cost of device-based VMMC varies depending on the type of device used. Current evidence primarily focuses on the PrePex and Shang Ring devices, leaving the costs of other VMMC devices unclear. The direct unit costs of surgical and device-based VMMC are approximately equivalent. However, the overall cost-effectiveness is highly sensitive to resource utilization rates. Device-based VMMC demonstrates greater cost reduction as resource utilization increases, leading to more apparent cost savings compared to the surgical approach. Nevertheless, the minimum resource utilization threshold required to achieve cost savings remains uncertain. For instance, a hypothetical PrePex-only site with low resource utilization may not achieve cost savings due to underutilization. As site capacity utilization improves, the per-unit cost differences between sites diminish. A cost-analysis study by Duffy in 2013 investigated future cost savings resulting from HIV infections averted (HIA) through VMMC. Conducted in Uganda, the study reported average unit costs and cost-effectiveness data for the PrePex device compared to the surgical approach among adult males aged 18 years and older. The sample size included 10,625 participants, with 10,000 undergoing surgical VMMC and 625 using the PrePex device. The study highlighted that unit costs and cost-effectiveness are highly sensitive to resource utilization rates. However, it did not evaluate the unit cost of demand creation. Additionally, the study was conducted from a service provider perspective and did not account for client time or costs incurred by clients receiving the service. The cost-effectiveness of the PrePex device was assessed by comparing the unit cost of circumcision with the estimated discounted savings from future care and treatment costs avoided due to HIV infections averted. PrePex has a unit cost 35% higher than the current surgical method. After accounting for future cost savings, it is 2% less cost-effective than the surgical approach. Overall, in terms of direct unit costs, device-based VMMC using PrePex can be considered cost-effective based on consistent findings from several cost-effectiveness studies (e.g., Bratt 2013, Duffy 2013, Kim 2015, Njeuhmeli 2014, Obiero 2013, Schutte 2016, Tshimanga 2016). If VMMC were scaled up, device-based VMMC could significantly lower average total costs compared to the surgical approach, as the former utilizes staff and other fixed resources more intensively (Bratt, 2013). Comparing the cost of performing circumcisions to the future cost savings from potentially averted HIV infections, PrePex-VMMC is only slightly less cost-effective than the surgical method. Regarding health equity, no evidence was identified on the impact of device-based VMMC on health equity. Subgroups or subpopulations that may be disadvantaged in receiving device-based VMMC or for whom device-based VMMC may be less effective for non-physiological reasons were not identified. In terms of feasibility, no studies were found investigating legal or bureaucratic constraints, barriers to implementation or sustainability, misuse or abuse of recommendations, or healthcare ethics related to implementing device-based VMMC recommendations. For younger adolescent boys aged 10–14 years, who are at future risk of HIV infection through heterosexual intercourse, VMMC (device-based or conventional surgical) performed at this age, when genitalia are not yet physically mature or the foreskin is not retractable, was compared to delaying VMMC until age 15 or older. Outcomes assessed included adequate removal of the foreskin, cosmesis, psychological distress, and pain during preparation, the procedure itself, or afterward.
